A few reasons why doing auto stuff might not be a good idea:

  • When we do a job and charge you, we charge based on the following things:
    • Our knowledge - you don't accurately diagnose problems with a few youtube searches, you learn through experience.
    • Parts - we make a markup on parts. Auto parts stores sell to you with this markup, but to us they sell without (see below).
    • Labor - actual work done. This is usually hourly and significantly more than wage (say $100 an hour). This of course isn't our take home (fun fact: mechanics make less than teachers) - this is usually how we consider paying for things like power, heating during the winter months, maintenence for our equipment, tools, etc.

  • Tools cost money - as a shop we can invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in tools.

  • If you don't know much, you can't just get an accurate fix from the internet. As an experienced mechanic, I can guess what the problem is based on symptoms and then confirm or reject my hypothesis through further diagnoses. Of course, some shops are just part changers who change parts until the problem goes away.

  • Parts at auto stores are often sold at "list" price incl. tax. As a shop, we get parts at "net" price without sales tax (which we are obligated to pass to the consumer). We also make money on the parts due to the difference between list and net price, where as auto parts stores directly make that profit. As a mechanic I can get parts at list and just pay the sales tax to the shop while the shop makes $0 markup.

  • Again on part stores - prices vary A LOT. A reverse switch for my car was $45 from autozone, or $12 from the manufacturer (yes, OEM was 1/4th the price!). Some stores cost more for some things and less for others. It's just how it goes. We as the shop know where to get cheap parts or quality parts and at the right price. Some of our stores are absolutely horrible sources for CV axles, but said store also can get oil of the same brand cheaper than the other store.

  • When shit goes wrong (such as we break something on accident or we get the wrong parts), we know exactly what to do. If a rattle clip on the brakes goes missing, we know how to deal with it. Most people don't know what a rattle clip is or how it goes.

Now reasons for you to do your own work:

  • Oil changes are the easiest thing to do - the hardest part is disposing of the oil properly. Just drain the stuff, remove the filter, prime the new filter, put it on, and fill the engine up till the dipstick reads full, run the engine for a minute, check the oil again and add as necessary.

  • Brakes are also pretty easy, at least discs are. A 5 minute youtube video could mostly explain how to do your brakes.

  • You save money (as with all things you do yourself) of course at the expense of time and lack of knowledge (how valuable is your time?)

  • You don't trust other people with your car (I don't blame you)

  • Some shops are legitimately run by retards - and in all honestly, a lot of dealerships are like this - they hire young people right out of tech school who want the scanner to tell them exactly what to fix and how - many of these kids are people who are duped by high automotive expenses into thinking they can make a lot of money.

  • Some shops charge out the ass for simple things - I understand a nearby Mercedes dealership charges $300 just to put the car on the lift - ignoring any work done. Many shops charge a fee to use their scanner (which on one hand makes sense, since good scanners cost a ton of money). Most cases a cheap $30 code scanner will be enough.

TL;DR: Work on your own car, just don't think mechanics are ripping you off and be very aware of what you're doing.
